title: What would happen if an AI agent interfered with a Canadian election?
summary: There are currently no provisions in Canada's electoral laws to address the prospect of AI agents acting without human direction trying to meddle in Canada's elections, says Canada's chief electoral…

image.caption: Chief Electoral Officer Stéphane Perrault, seen last year, testified before MPs on Thursday about AI and Canada's elections. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

There are currently no provisions in Canada's electoral laws to address the prospect of AI agents acting without human direction trying to meddle in Canada's elections, says Canada's chief electoral officer.
Chief electoral officer says there are no legal provisions to deal with AI acting alone

There are currently no provisions in Canada's electoral laws to address the prospect of artificial intelligence acting without human direction trying to meddle in Canada's elections, says Canada's chief electoral officer.
Speaking to CBC News after testifying before a parliamentary committee, Stéphane Perrault said he is not aware of any provision in the Elections Act that would cover such a scenario.
"The law is based on human accountability for their acts, civil or criminal," he said. "So, it always falls back to what are the people or the corporate entities behind that."

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly sophisticated, it raises questions of what would happen if an AI agent, which can independently decide to take specific actions, tried to influence a Canadian election but it couldn't be proved that there was a human in the loop or that a human gave it inappropriate direction.
"It's a really significant question," said Perrault. "What is the civil and criminal accountability of AI agents?"
Voters face 'challenge' of evolving AI use in elections, says chief electoral officer
Perrault's comments came after he faced similar questions during Thursday's meeting of the House of Commons committee on procedure and House affairs.
"We are seeing AI agents that are taking decisions that do not appear to be human driven. There's no person behind it," said Liberal MP Anita Vandenbeld.

"If an AI agent were to contravene the Election Act but it can't be shown that it was an individual — it was rather the AI agent making decisions based on their own…. This is in the future, I know, but how can you hold a computer to account for something?"
Perrault said Elections Canada's website is constantly under attack but there have not been any breaches.
"Your question is a very deep one," he said. "It goes well beyond electoral issues."
'A great hypothetical question'
Commissioner of Canada Elections Caroline Simard said it is something her office would have to examine more closely.
"It's a great hypothetical question," she said. "I would say right now we have new powers that can help us act on the current developments of AI but we would have to look into it further."

Vandenbeld also wanted to know what elections officials are doing to ensure that AI platforms can include credible information from their websites in their answer to questions from users. She said during the recent Quebec election, AI tools picked up information from one particular website because it was easier for them to read than more formal websites.
"It wasn't nefarious but it could have been," she said. "It could have been a foreign agent that would put this kind of information [online]."
Perrault said his office is working with AI platforms to ensure that Elections Canada's website can be picked up by the platforms.
"We are beginning to engage with AI platforms to ensure that our information is formatted, that it is presented in a manner that will be picked up by the platforms," he said.
"This is an emerging area for us but it is a very important one."

blocks.text: Conservative Rob Moore asked what Perrault and Simard are doing to counter any attempts to use AI to interfere in elections, pointing out with close votes, even a little bit of interference could have an impact on the results.
"Training, training, training," said Simard.

Perrault said attempts at foreign interference did take place during the 2025 election, such as attempts to target Conservative candidate Joe Tay, but it is difficult to ascertain impact and influence on elections.

"I'm not aware of any information or any evidence of impact on the election, so it's a negative statement in that regard," Perrault told the committee. "But it speaks at the same time to the importance of fighting these attempts. Whether or not they have impact, they do undermine trust in the electoral process."
Simard said her office is still investigating complaints received regarding the 2025 federal election but did not provide details of those investigations.
